projects.name: OTHMODE (othmode.mythosprod.xyz)
projects.purpose: The OTHMODE control platform: the per-command control contract for Claude work on Mythos. A command activates it only when it contains the standalone keyword `othmode`; activation selects a control contract and grants no permission of any kind. Surfaces the command library, skills, tools, providers, memory, the Evolution layer and — since 2026-08-26 — a persistent Task Report for every activated command, readable as the fourth source of the unified Command History.

projects.headline: Live at https://othmode.mythosprod.xyz since 2026-08-26. Built over the MCC-1 runtime rather than as a second system: one process on a single loopback port, same auth, CSRF and secret gate, no new event store. Task Reports add an append-only tasks/records.jsonl stream to the existing OTHMODE store and a fourth source to the existing Command History. As of 7252de2 the Command History and every Task Report are PUBLIC READS — no session, login link or token — while every write stays authenticated and secret-gated; anonymous readers get the full narrative with infrastructure detail masked by a read-side projection, since the append-only store cannot be rewritten to be publishable. Suites othmode-3 94/0 and othmode-2 157/0 on the production host. Per-command activation replaced the global switch in PR #87; the keyword confers no privilege.

Finding from the first restore test, recorded so it does not cost someone time during a real recovery. The restored media set contains manifest.json and media/ but NOT checksums.sha256, even though media-backup/manifest.json names it under integrity.checksums_file with its sha256. That looks like a gap and is not one. offhost-backup.js mediaEntries() reads checksums.sha256 as the INDEX of what to ship and folds every one of its 71 hashes into the top-level off-host manifest, which is what restore-verify checks against; the file itself is therefore redundant as an object and is deliberately not pushed. Integrity off-host does not depend on it. A human performing a manual recovery without the tool should verify against the restored manifest.json, not look for checksums.sha256 — recorded in ops/backup/README.md §4.

THE DEPLOYMENT SCRIPT REPORTED FAILURE ON A DEPLOYMENT THAT SUCCEEDED, and the defect was mine (OTH-2026-00018 wrote it, OTH-2026-00019 found and fixed it). Its step-5 smoke tests used `curl -I`. The upstream is GET-only and answers HEAD with 405 by design, so the primary 'HTTPS 200' check failed against a healthy site. Proven from the vhost's own access log, which records the script's probes from 51.68.226.211 at 20:01:52Z: HEAD / 405, three times. A second check was worse than wrong — it read Content-Type from the HEAD 405 response, which is also application/json, so it PASSED for entirely the wrong reason and would have false-greened a broken API. A third asserted POST /api/health returns 403 at the edge; it returns 405, because an exact-match nginx location beats a regex one and `location = /api/health` did not inherit the `limit_except` from `location ~ ^/api/`. FIXED: every probe is now a GET using `-D- -o /dev/null` so the checks read the headers users actually get; the write-refusal property is asserted twice and separately — 403 at the edge on a regex-governed /api/ path, and 403-or-405 on /api/health — so neither can hide the other; and a redirect-target check was added. The template now repeats limit_except inside the exact-match block so future installs refuse writes uniformly at the edge. THE LIVE VHOST STILL LACKS THAT LINE: writes to /api/health are refused by the upstream's 405 rather than by nginx, one layer later than every other path. That is a defence-in-depth gap, not an exposure — the request is still refused and nothing is written — and closing it needs a root edit, because this script deliberately never rewrites a certbot-managed vhost.
